danish.title: Fjerde bog (1806) — Kapitel 15
paragraphs: At sige »i morgen« og bevare en værdig tone var ikke svært, men at gå hjem alene, se sine søstre, sin bror, sin mor og far, tilstå og bede om penge, han ingen ret havde til efter at have givet sit ord — det var forfærdeligt.

Derhjemme var de endnu ikke gået i seng. De unge mennesker var efter at være kommet hjem fra teatret blevet færdige med aftensmaden og sad samlet om klaveret. Så snart Nikolaj trådte ind, blev han indhyllet i den poetiske kærlighedsatmosfære, der gennemsyrede familien Rostovs hjem den vinter, og som nu efter Dolokhov s frieri og Iogels bal syntes at være blevet endnu tættere omkring Sonja og Natasja, ligesom luften før et tordenvejr. Sonja og Natasja sad i de lyseblå kjoler, de havde båret i teatret, kønne og bevidste om det, ved klaveret, lykkelige og smilende. Vera spillede skak med Sjinsjin i dagligstuen. Den gamle grevinde ventede på sin mands og søns hjemkomst og lagde kabale sammen med den gamle hofdame, der boede hos dem. Denisov sad ved klaveret med tindrende øjne og pjusket hår, slog akkorder med sine korte fingre, strakte benene bagud og rullede med øjnene, mens han sang med sin lille, hæse, men rene stemme nogle vers kaldet »Tryllerske«, som han selv havde digtet og nu forsøgte at sætte musik til:
Tryllerske, sig, hvad er det for en magt, der kalder mig til min forladte lyre? Hvad er den gnist, der sætter sjælen i brand? Hvad er den fryd, der får min finger til at dirre?
Han sang med lidenskabelig stemme og rettede sine funklende, sorte agatøjne mod den forskræmte og lykkelige Natasja.
»Pragtfuldt! Fremragende!« udbrød Natasja. »Endnu et vers,« sagde hun uden at lægge mærke til Nikolaj.
»Alt er som altid hos dem,« tænkte Nikolaj og så ind i dagligstuen, hvor han fik øje på Vera og sin mor sammen med den gamle dame.
»Nå, og her er Nikolaj!« råbte Natasja og løb hen til ham.
»Er far hjemme?« spurgte han.
»Jeg er så glad for, at du er kommet!« sagde Natasja uden at svare ham. »Vi morer os så dejligt! Vasilij Dmitritj bliver en dag ekstra for min skyld! Vidste du det?«
»Nej, far er ikke kommet hjem endnu,« sagde Sonja.
»Nikolaj, er du kommet? Kom herind, min dreng!« kaldte den gamle grevinde fra dagligstuen.

Nikolaj gik ind til hende, kyssede hendes hånd, satte sig tavst ved hendes bord og begyndte at se på hendes hænder, der ordnede kortene. Fra danseværelset hørtes stadig latter og glade stemmer, der forsøgte at overtale Natasja til at synge.
»Godt nok! Godt nok!« råbte Denisov. »Det nytter ikke at komme med undskyldninger nu! Det er din tur til at synge barcarollen — jeg bønfalder dig!«
Grevinden så på sin tavse søn.
»Hvad er der i vejen?« spurgte hun.
»Åh, ingenting,« sagde han, som om han var træt af til stadighed at blive spurgt om det samme. »Kommer far snart hjem?«
»Det regner jeg med.«
»Alt er som altid hos dem. De aner ingenting! Hvor skal jeg gå hen?« tænkte Nikolaj og gik igen ind i danseværelset, hvor klaveret stod.
Sonja sad ved klaveret og spillede forspillet til Denisovs yndlingsbarcarolle. Natasja gjorde sig klar til at synge. Denisov betragtede hende med henrykte øjne.
Nikolaj begyndte at gå frem og tilbage i stuen.
»Hvorfor vil de have hende til at synge? Hvordan kan hun synge? Der er da ingenting at være glad for!« tænkte han.
Sonja slog den første akkord i forspillet an.

»Herregud, jeg er en ruineret og vanæret mand! En kugle gennem hjernen er det eneste, der er tilbage — ikke at synge!« fór det gennem hans tanker. »Gå? Men hvorhen? Det er lige meget — lad dem synge!«
Han fortsatte med at gå frem og tilbage i stuen, mens han dystert betragtede Denisov og pigerne og undgik deres blikke.
»Nikolenka, hvad er der i vejen?« Sonjas øjne, der var fæstet på ham, syntes at spørge. Hun mærkede straks, at der var sket ham noget.

Nikolaj vendte sig fra hende. Natasja havde med sit hurtige instinkt også øjeblikkeligt bemærket sin brors tilstand. Men skønt hun lagde mærke til det, var hun selv så højt oppe i det øjeblik, så langt fra sorg, tristhed eller selvbebrejdelse, at hun bevidst bedrog sig selv, som unge mennesker ofte gør. »Nej, jeg er for lykkelig lige nu til at lade min fornøjelse ødelægge af medlidenhed med nogens sorg,« følte hun og sagde til sig selv: »Nej, jeg tager fejl, han må nok føle sig glad, ligesom jeg.«
»Nå, Sonja!« sagde hun og gik helt ud midt i stuen, hvor hun mente, akustikken var bedst.
Med løftet hoved og slappe, nedhængende arme, som balletdanserinder gør, gik Natasja med energiske skridt fra hæl til tå ud midt på gulvet og stillede sig op.
»Ja, det er mig!« syntes hun at sige som svar på det henrykte blik, hvormed Denisov fulgte hende.
»Og hvad er hun så glad for?« tænkte Nikolaj og så på sin søster. »Hvorfor keder hun sig ikke og skammer sig ikke?«

Natasja tog den første tone, hendes strube svulmede, brystet hævede sig, øjnene blev alvorlige. I det øjeblik var hun uvidende om sine omgivelser, og fra hendes smilende læber flød toner, som hvem som helst kan frembringe med de samme intervaller og holde lige så længe, men som lader én kold tusind gange og den tusind og første gang giver rystelser og får tårerne til at trille.

Natasja havde den vinter for første gang begyndt at synge seriøst, hovedsagelig fordi Denisov var så begejstret for hendes sang. Hun sang ikke længere som et barn, der var ikke længere det komiske, barnlige, omhyggelige ved hendes sang, som der havde været før; men hun sang endnu ikke godt, som alle kendere, der hørte hende, sagde: »Stemmen er ikke uddannet, men det er en smuk stemme, der bør uddannes.« Det sagde de dog som regel først et stykke tid efter, at hun var holdt op med at synge. Mens den utrænede stemme med dens ukorrekte vejrtrækning og anstrengte overgange lød, sagde selv kenderne ingenting, men nød den blot og ønskede at høre den igen. I hendes stemme var der en jomfruelig friskhed, en ubevidsthed om egne kræfter og en endnu utrænet fløjlsblødhed, der smeltede så fuldstændig sammen med hendes mangel på sangteknik, at det virkede, som om intet i den stemme kunne ændres uden at ødelægge den.

»Hvad er det?« tænkte Nikolaj og lyttede med vidt åbne øjne. »Hvad er der sket med hende? Hvor synger hun i dag!« Og pludselig samlede hele verden sig for ham om forventningen om den næste tone, den næste frase, og alt i verden var delt i tre taktslag: »Oh mio crudele affetto« ... En, to, tre ... en, to, tre ... En ... »Oh mio crudele affetto« ... En, to, tre ... En. »Åh, dette meningsløse liv!« tænkte Nikolaj. »Al den elendighed og pengene og Dolokhov og æren — det er alt sammen vrøvl ... men det her er virkeligt ... Nå, Natasja, nå, min skat! Nå, min elskede! Hvordan tager hun den si? Hun tog den! Gudske lov!« Og uden at lægge mærke til, at han selv sang med for at understøtte tonen, sang han en sekund og en terts under den høje tone. »Åh, Gud! Hvor fint! Tog jeg den virkelig? Hvor heldigt!« tænkte han.

Åh, hvordan den akkord vibrerede, og hvor bevæget var det fineste i Rostovs sjæl! Og dette noget var adskilt fra alt andet i verden og hævet over alt i verden. »Hvad var tab og Dolokhov og æresord? ... Alt sammen vrøvl! Man kunne slå ihjel og røve og alligevel være lykkelig ...«

english.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: Saying "tomorrow" and keeping up a dignified front wasn't difficult. But going home alone, facing his sisters, brother, mother, and father, confessing what he'd done, and asking for money he had no right to after giving his word of honor — that was terrible.

At home, they hadn't gone to bed yet. The young people had come back from the theater, had supper, and were gathered around the clavichord. The moment Nicholas walked in, he was enveloped by the romantic atmosphere that had pervaded the Rostov household all winter — and which, after Dolokhov's proposal and Iogel's ball, seemed to have grown even thicker around Sonya and Natasha, like the air before a thunderstorm. Sonya and Natasha were standing by the clavichord in the light blue dresses they'd worn to the theater, looking pretty and aware of it, happy and smiling. Vera was playing chess with Shinshin in the drawing room. The old countess, waiting for her husband and son to come home, was playing patience with the elderly gentlewoman who lived with the family. Denisov, his eyes sparkling and his hair disheveled, sat at the clavichord striking chords with his short fingers, his legs thrown back and his eyes rolling as he sang in his small, husky, but true voice some verses he'd composed called "Enchantress," for which he was trying to find the right music:
Enchantress, say, to my forsaken lyre / What magic power is this recalls me still? / What spark has set my inmost soul on fire, / What is this bliss that makes my fingers thrill?
He sang with passion, his sparkling dark eyes fixed on the frightened and happy Natasha.
"Wonderful! Brilliant!" exclaimed Natasha. "Another verse!" she said, without even noticing Nicholas.
"Everything's the same with them," thought Nicholas, glancing into the drawing room where he saw Vera and his mother with the old lady.
"Oh, Nicholas is here!" cried Natasha, running up to him.
"Is Papa home?" he asked.
"I'm so glad you've come!" said Natasha, ignoring his question. "We're having such a wonderful time! Vasili Dmitrich is staying an extra day just for me! Did you know?"
"No, Papa isn't back yet," said Sonya.
"Nicholas, is that you? Come here, darling!" called the old countess from the drawing room.
Nicholas went to her, kissed her hand, and sat down silently at her table, watching her hands arrange the cards. From the music room came laughter and cheerful voices urging Natasha to sing.
"All wight! All wight!" Denisov shouted. "No more excuses! It's your turn to sing the ba'cawolla — I beg you!"
The countess glanced at her silent son.
"What's wrong?" she asked.
"Oh, nothing," he said, as though tired of being asked the same question over and over. "Will Papa be home soon?"
"I think so."
"Everything's the same with them. They know nothing about it! Where can I go?" Nicholas thought, and he went back to the music room where the clavichord stood.
Sonya was at the clavichord, playing the prelude to Denisov's favorite barcarolle. Natasha was getting ready to sing. Denisov was watching her with adoring eyes.
Nicholas began pacing up and down the room.
"Why do they want her to sing? How can she sing? There's nothing to be happy about!" he thought.
Sonya struck the first chord of the prelude.
"My God, I'm a ruined and disgraced man! A bullet through my brain is the only thing left for me — not singing!" his thoughts ran on. "Leave? But where? It doesn't matter — let them sing!"
He continued pacing the room, looking darkly at Denisov and the girls, avoiding their eyes.
"Nikolenka, what's wrong?" Sonya's eyes seemed to ask. She noticed at once that something had happened to him.

Nicholas turned away from her. Natasha too, with her quick instincts, had instantly noticed her brother's state. But though she saw it, she was so full of joy at that moment, so far from any sorrow, sadness, or self-reproach, that she deliberately fooled herself, as young people often do. "No, I'm too happy right now to let anyone's suffering spoil it," she felt, and told herself: "No, I must be wrong — he's probably just as happy as I am."
"Ready, Sonya!" she said, walking to the very center of the room, where she believed the acoustics were best.
She lifted her head, let her arms drop limply at her sides like a ballet dancer, and, rising energetically from her heels to her toes, stepped to the middle of the room and stood still.
"Yes, this is me!" she seemed to say, responding to the rapt gaze with which Denisov followed her.
"And what is she so pleased about?" Nicholas thought, looking at his sister. "Why doesn't she feel gloomy and ashamed?"

Natasha took her first note. Her throat swelled, her chest rose, her eyes grew serious. In that moment she was oblivious to everything around her, and from her smiling lips flowed sounds that anyone can produce at the same intervals and sustain for the same duration — but which leave you cold a thousand times, and on the thousand-and-first time make you tremble and weep.

That winter, Natasha had begun singing seriously for the first time, mainly because Denisov took such delight in her voice. She no longer sang like a child — the comical, painstaking, childish quality was gone. But she didn't yet sing well, as every expert who heard her would say: "It's an untrained voice, but a beautiful one that needs proper training." Except they usually said this some time after she'd finished. While that untrained voice was actually sounding — with its imperfect breathing and labored transitions — even the critics said nothing. They simply listened with pleasure and wanted to hear more. In her voice there was a virginal freshness, an unawareness of her own gifts, and a velvety softness that had not yet been shaped by art — and these qualities blended so perfectly with her lack of technique that it seemed nothing about that voice could be changed without ruining it.

"What is this?" thought Nicholas, listening with wide eyes. "What's happened to her? How she's singing today!" And suddenly the whole world narrowed for him to the anticipation of the next note, the next phrase, and everything divided into three beats: "Oh mio crudele affetto"... One, two, three... one, two, three... One... "Oh mio crudele affetto"... One, two, three... One. "Oh, this senseless life of ours!" thought Nicholas. "All this misery, and money, and Dolokhov, and anger, and honor — it's all nonsense... but this is real... Come on, Natasha, come on, darling! Come on, sweetheart! How will she take that high note? She took it! Thank God!" And without realizing he was singing, he added a harmony — a second and then a third below the high note. "Oh God, how beautiful! Did I really hit that note? How wonderful!" he thought.

Oh, how that chord vibrated, and how deeply it stirred the finest part of Rostov's soul! And this was something apart from everything else in the world, something above everything in the world. "What are losses, and Dolokhov, and words of honor?... All nonsense! A person could kill and rob and still be happy..."
